core: Historical and global study of art, architecture and archaeological/material culture
Visual and textual interpretation, art-historical theory and researched cultural inquiry
Art, objects and media as cultural representation, heritage and identity
adjacent: Heritage, ownership, political power and cultural identity
Art, visual media and environmental humanities
questions: How do images, objects and museums construct and contest cultural identities?
How do visual representations make environmental change and ecological awareness meaningful?

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
trace: Actual Western art chronology, close painting analysis and on-site art research supply a direct art-historical and visual-method foundation.
Artefacts, production, visual/material evidence and community identities supply direct archaeological/material-culture inquiry, not a complete architecture survey.
Actual material culture of Greek community/democracy supports ancient art and heritage interpretation; no Roman survey is inferred.
Western African visual traditions, religious/social meanings and colonial collecting/restitution directly sustain global art and contested heritage.
Actual Renaissance art and architecture through Mediterranean/global exchange supply direct early-modern art study, within description-only limits.
Modern and contemporary art, avant-gardes and museum institutions directly connect visual practices with display, reception and cultural change.
Athenian art, archaeology, myth, civic identity and participatory cultural work support specific ancient heritage and public cultural meaning.
Actual history of art history from the sixteenth century to contemporary interpretation, identity and global debates sustains disciplinary historiography and methods, within the official description.
Close reading, symbolism, narrative perspective and introductory film adaptation provide specific interpretive tools alongside visual-culture study, not art-history survey substitution.

Classical and global mythic narratives, transmission, gender-focused interpretation and cross-cultural adaptation support interpretation of cultural stories; no complete Christian iconography sequence is supplied.
Actual medium specificity, image/sound/editing and text-film adaptation provide sustained visual/narrative analysis; a more concrete core contribution than a general philosophy survey.
Actual cinematic form, film history and audiovisual interpretation ground visual-culture/media analysis, with tangible methods relevant to cultural representation.
Material media technologies and historical theories of communication/knowledge/memory support interpretation of visual culture; not dedicated photography history by inference.
Actual ecocritical image/film/sound analysis studies representation of human-nonhuman relations and ecological change; no dedicated seventeenth-century Dutch landscape module is claimed.
Actual American media/race, archival/visual sources and marginalized storytelling support the interpretation of cultural power and representation; not an American art survey.
Documentary form, ethnographic/nonfiction representation, interviewing and production ethics support researched public interpretation of visual/cultural evidence.
Industrialization, imperialism, decolonization and cultural/political change supply specific historical contexts for modern visual cultures, not art-period teaching.
Imperial legitimacy, ideology and cultural legacies provide comparative historical context for cultural exchange, collecting and ownership; not an architecture sequence.

Actual Indigenous cultural expression, exhibitions/film, arts-based collaboration and public history support cultural identity and heritage interpretation; not a substitute for the external American Art survey.
Current description2 supports full historical research, critical sources, interdisciplinary method and a substantial paper; no archived Walcheren outline or guaranteed art topic is used.
Moral arguments about care, rights, death/meaning and judgment provide specific ethical tools for heritage ownership, representation and ecological responsibility; not aesthetics teaching.
Actual identity, othering, social boundaries and colonial formation of social theory support analysis of cultural representation and heritage communities.
Actual visual/documentary research, interviewing, ethnography, coding and reflexivity support empirical interpretation of heritage/media and cultural practices.
Public spheres, hegemony, civil society and empirical cultural/public initiatives support inquiry into whose identities and values museums/media make public.

Authority, rights and historical/contemporary political arguments supply explicit normative concepts for cultural ownership and public representation; no dedicated heritage or decolonial-art course is inferred.
Cultural relativism, universality, dignity, religious/expression rights and case/argument analysis support contested cultural ownership and public cultural rights.
Actual colonial grievances, identity, transitional justice and reconciliation/arts connect heritage narratives to conflict and public memory.
Actual analysis of texts, films, exhibitions and protest art examines how climate representations are argued over; directly relevant to public visual meaning.
Actual climate processes/impacts and stakeholder/short-film communication supply the scientific and social object interpreted by environmental visual media; not landscape-art training.

Actual public participation, institutions, climate justice and policy narratives explain governance of the environmental changes and disputes represented in cultural/media inquiry; no architecture/design equivalence.
Actual environmental movements, anti-colonialism and justice provide substantive social stakes for ecological representation and protest, within official-description limits.

alternatives.label: Art history and visual culture
alternatives.concept: Historical study of actual art and material culture, art-historical methods and visual/narrative interpretation across selected global periods. Specific historical and social contexts support that art/visual anchor. It does not reproduce the complete architecture/period survey, iconography, field excursions or required thesis.
alternatives.labelReason: The label describes the actual complete curriculum and its relative art, interpretive, historical/social or environmental weight; no architecture/field/thesis equivalence.
progression: Current workbook schedule: exact 24/180, four per term, Year-1 PPD, actual planned offerings and earlier prerequisites. Foundations precede advanced art/media inquiry where feasible; open formal rules are retained.

alternatives.label: Heritage, identity and cultural power
alternatives.concept: Art, archaeology and museums anchor sustained inquiry into cultural ownership, colonial collecting, Indigenous expression, rights and public memory. Political/social analysis changes the educational emphasis while retaining real art-historical study.

alternatives.label: Art, visual media and environmental humanities
alternatives.concept: Actual art/heritage and visual-media methods are combined with ecocritical interpretation, climate communication, climate science and environmental justice/governance. The organizing problem is how environmental change becomes represented and contested; no technical planning course is relabelled as art.

candidates.label: Art, visual media and environmental humanities

selection.assessment: Three independently supported programmes: closest art/visual inquiry, heritage/public cultural power and environmental visual humanities. All retain an actual art/heritage anchor. Pairwise differences arise from substantive priorities, not substitutions to meet a threshold.

blocks: Historical art, architecture and material culture
No dedicated medieval visual-art survey is established by the selected UCR courses.
UCR modern art gives relevant period connections but is placed at the stronger twentieth-century relationship; no separate nineteenth-century survey is inferred.
No equivalent medieval-art field excursion/seminar is supplied.
Both examine Greek material/visual culture in historical and community context; Radboud additionally surveys Roman archaeology, while UCR focuses on early democracy.
No dedicated late-antique-to-Renaissance architecture sequence is supplied.
No dedicated modern global architecture survey is supplied.
Both study Renaissance visual art and historical context. UCR emphasizes Italian/Mediterranean/global exchange; Radboud includes broader European Renaissance/Baroque chronology.
Both study twentieth-century and contemporary visual art, movements and interpretation. UCR emphasizes museums/display and begins in the late nineteenth century.
Paris excursion and sustained situated study are distinct from UCR museum/visual inquiry.
No dedicated Asian architectural history/globalization sequence is supplied.
Native American cultural/visual work is a real contribution, not the external American Art survey.
Ethics or general philosophical reasoning does not establish a dedicated aesthetics curriculum.

Both develop actual visual analysis and historically grounded art inquiry. Radboud explicitly introduces art history as a discipline; UCR combines close painting analysis/on-site research with a broad Western art survey.
Art/literary research contributes writing, but no separate course is asserted as this first-year art-history seminar.
General visual analysis and myth do not establish the specific Christian/profane iconography and source sequence.
Both study the development and use of art-historical interpretive methods and historiography. Detailed theoretical selections and assessments differ.
Broad media-technology history does not establish dedicated photographic history and interpretation.
Required independent art-history thesis and supervision are distinct from scheduled methods/projects; optional UCR research remains additional to 180 EC.

Both examine how visual representation makes human/environment relations meaningful using environmental-humanities interpretation. Radboud specializes in seventeenth-century Dutch landscape images; UCR spans wider historical and contemporary image/film/sound contexts.
Two permitted whole Faculty of Arts minors remain restricted choice, with no invented selected subject package.
Both develop reflection, academic/personal competencies and future direction. UCR places its civic/academic development in Year 1; Radboud provides a final history-specific career/portfolio course.
Genuine 30-EC open study remains uninstantiated and is not assigned invented subject correspondence.

notes.text: UCR combines art history, archaeology, heritage and visual-media inquiry. Radboud supplies a more extensive art/architecture chronology, dedicated iconography, photography and excursions, and a required art-history thesis. The heritage and environmental programmes are broader related directions, not Radboud specialisations.

acceptance.claim: Actual UCR art, archaeological/heritage and visual-method study supports a broader Art History comparison and two evidenced related directions, without reproducing the complete external architecture/period, excursion or thesis formation.
acceptance.challengeMethod: Separately identified same-AI source-first final pass against actual adopted OER/current UCR content and exact finished records, not separate human or agent approval.

uncertainties.fact: The same 10-EC Paris code is repeated in the adopted ordinary B2/B3 tables. Only 170 distinct EC are supported; the other required 10 EC and their role remain unverified.

adverseResolutions.resolution: An authoritative correction replaces the repeated entry with a distinct art/architectural period, methods or practical course.
adverseResolutions.effectOnClaim: The unknown study stays excluded and may extend stated specialist gaps. It cannot remove the confirmed historical/method core or the actual substantial UCR art/visual response.

adverseResolutions.resolution: A genuinely distinct advanced Paris requirement or permitted choice explains the extra 10 EC.
adverseResolutions.effectOnClaim: Its content and separate credit remain unverified and unmatched. The limited broader academic claim does not promise Paris/field or full-degree equivalence and survives.

audience.programmeDescription: Art History at Radboud studies artworks, architecture and visual culture in their historical contexts, from antiquity to the present. It combines visual analysis, art-historical theories and methods, museum visits and independent research.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR offers art history and visual culture, with related programmes in heritage/cultural power and environmental visual humanities. All contain substantial art and archaeological/heritage study. Radboud offers more extensive period and architecture study, dedicated iconography/photography, excursions and an independent art-history thesis. Its adopted table repeats the same Paris course; the unverified 10 EC are excluded from this qualified comparison.

curriculum.limitation: The degree is 180 EC. This list accounts for 170 distinct EC because the same 10-EC Paris course appears in both year 2 and year 3. The remaining 10 EC need clarification. Future Florence and Kunstwerelden courses are not treated as current replacements. This is a partial list, not a complete degree pathway. Required first-year mentoring, the Dutch academic-language diagnostic and second-year personal/professional development add no credits. Attendance applies to mentoring and seminars.

comparisonScope.label: Qualified academic comparison
